en.title: Earning and spending
en.summary: Wages, prices, budgets and saving, with the language of numbers and approximations.

paragraphs: Everyone has to think about money. This lesson gives you the words for earning, spending and saving and shows how to talk about budgets without being too direct.
Two friends who share a flat in Liverpool discuss their monthly budget.

lines.speaker: Gina
lines.text: How much do you earn a month?

lines.speaker: Hal
lines.text: About two thousand pounds, before tax. After tax it's nearer sixteen hundred.

lines.speaker: Gina
lines.text: And how much do you spend on rent?

lines.speaker: Hal
lines.text: Nearly half. I try to save a little each month, but it isn't easy.

lines.speaker: Gina
lines.text: Have you thought about making a budget?

lines.speaker: Hal
lines.text: I have, but I never stick to it.

lines.speaker: Gina
lines.text: If you wrote down everything you spent, you'd see where the money goes.

lines.speaker: Hal
lines.text: You're right. I'll start next month.

paragraphs: **1. Earn, spend, save and waste form a family of verbs.** Learn them together with their typical objects. See Introduction to Grammar: Verbs and verb phrases.

blocks.html:
VerbMeaningExample
earnreceive pay for workI earn two thousand a month.
spenduse moneyI spend half on rent.
savekeep for laterI save a little each month.
wasteuse badlyDon't waste money on things you don't need.

paragraphs: **2. Approximate numbers with about, nearly and roughly.** They soften a figure so it does not sound too exact. See Introduction to Grammar: Adverbs.

blocks.html:
WordExample
aboutabout two thousand pounds
nearlynearly half
roughlyroughly a third
just over / just underjust under sixteen hundred

items: Salary is paid monthly; wage is paid hourly or weekly.
Gross means before tax; net means after tax.
A budget is a plan for spending; to stick to a budget means to follow it.
Make ends meet means to have just enough money to live.

paragraphs: Asking a person how much they earn is considered rude in Britain and the United States, although friends sometimes talk about it. Salaries are often quoted per year, while wages are quoted per hour.
